stem_html:
Critics who call Isabella Stewart Gardner's museum eccentric miss how ______ its arrangement is. No label tells the visitor what to think, but a Titian hangs where the light will reach it for one hour in March, and a chair is placed so that the only comfortable view of the room is the one Gardner preferred.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "ornate", "trap": "vocab-collocation"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "calculated"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "instructive", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "conventional", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The contrast is with “eccentric,” not with “plain.” The blank has to name what the critics missed, and what they missed is design, not decoration.
  • A museum word that fits the setting and not the sentence. “Ornate” belongs to the world of Titians and gilt chairs, which is why it is chosen; nothing in the sentence is about ornament.
  • The first clause after the blank denies instruction. “No label tells the visitor what to think” rules out the choice that says the arrangement teaches.

Why A is wrong Ornate describes surfaces. The evidence offered concerns where things are placed and when the light falls, which is planning rather than decoration.

Why B is right Both examples are decisions made in advance to control what the visitor experiences: a Titian hangs where the light will reach it for one hour in March, and the chair fixes the preferred view. Calculated names exactly that.

Why C is wrong The sentence says no label tells the visitor what to think. An arrangement can be deliberate without instructing, and this passage insists on the distinction.

Why D is wrong Conventional is the opposite of what the sentence concedes. The critics call the museum eccentric, and the writer does not deny its strangeness, only its aimlessness.

stem_html:
The committee's final report was ______ in a way its members had not intended: by declining to recommend either proposal, it left the decision exactly where it had been eighteen months earlier, with the department heads who had asked for guidance.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"premature","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"consequential","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"C","content":"inert"},{"letter":"D","content":"impartial","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “In a way its members had not intended” suggests an effect. The rest of the sentence describes an absence of effect, and the phrase misleads a reader who stops at the colon.
  • The neutral reading is available and unearned. Declining to recommend either proposal does sound impartial, but impartiality is not something a committee fails to intend.
  • Timing is never mentioned. Eighteen months is offered as a measure of wasted time, not of prematurity.

Why A is wrong Premature would mean issued too early. The complaint is that eighteen months produced nothing, not that the report arrived before its time.

Why B is wrong Consequential means having significant effects, and the sentence describes a report that changed nothing: the decision sat exactly where it had been.

Why C is right Inert names doing nothing while appearing to act. The unintended quality is precisely that the report, for all its length, moved nothing, which is what the second half of the sentence spells out.

Why D is wrong True of the behavior described and wrong for the sentence, because impartiality would be an intended virtue rather than an unintended outcome the members would regret.

stem_html:
Ecologists once treated the seed bank in desert soil as ______ store, drawn down in dry years and refilled in wet ones. Long-term plots have complicated that picture: some species' seeds germinate only after two consecutive wet winters, so a decade of single wet years leaves the bank untouched.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"an inexhaustible","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"B","content":"a contested","trap":"vocab-collocation"},{"letter":"C","content":"a fragile","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"D","content":"a uniform"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The correction tells you what the old view assumed. The complication is that species differ in what triggers them, so the discarded assumption is sameness across species.
  • Fragility is the ecology word one expects. Nothing in the sentence concerns how easily the seed bank is destroyed.
  • Draw-down language suggests a reservoir. That pulls toward “inexhaustible,” and the passage explicitly says the store is drawn down.

Why A is wrong Too strong, and contradicted by the same sentence, which has the store drawn down in dry years.

Why B is wrong Contested describes disagreement among scientists, but the sentence says ecologists once treated it that way, meaning the view was settled rather than disputed.

Why C is wrong Fragile speaks to vulnerability, and the passage's revision concerns germination triggers, not the risk of losing the bank.

Why D is right The old model treated the whole bank as one thing that fills and empties together. The correction is that some species' seeds germinate only after two consecutive wet winters, so the parts behave differently from one another.

stem_html:
A linguist proposed that a language's word order tends to become fixed as its case endings erode, because word order then carries the information the endings used to. A colleague objected that the two changes might simply share a cause, such as heavy contact with adult second-language learners, rather than one driving the other.

Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the linguist's proposal against the colleague's objection?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "In two related languages with comparable histories of adult-learner contact, the one whose case endings eroded first fixed its word order roughly a century later, and the one whose endings survived retained free word order."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Languages with heavy adult-learner contact are, on average, more likely to have both fixed word order and reduced case marking than languages without it.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Speakers of languages with fixed word order report finding case endings difficult to learn.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Several languages with rich case systems also have fixed word order.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Correlation is what the objection already grants. Choice B reports exactly the joint occurrence the colleague explains by a common cause, so it cannot decide between them.
  • Holding the confound fixed is the move. The only way to separate the two accounts is to compare cases matched on contact and see whether the order of the changes still follows the proposal.
  • A counterexample dressed as support. Choice D describes languages that have both features without the erosion, which if anything weakens the proposed mechanism.

Why A is right It matches the languages on the confound the colleague proposed, heavy contact with adult second-language learners, and then finds the sequence the proposal predicts: erosion first, fixing about a century later, and no fixing where the endings survived. With the confound held constant, the timing is left to the mechanism.

Why B is wrong This is the correlation the objection is built on. Both accounts predict it, so it separates nothing.

Why C is wrong Learner difficulty is a possible reason endings erode. It says nothing about whether the erosion drives the word order or whether both follow from contact.

Why D is wrong Rich case systems alongside fixed order shows the two features can coexist, which does not support a claim that one produces the other.

They concluded that the zinc-rich primer outperforms the others chiefly at the plate edges, where coatings are thinnest, rather than across flat surfaces.

Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to support the team's conclusion?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The conclusion has two halves and most choices serve one. “Better at the edges” needs the edge gap; “rather than across flat surfaces” needs the flat-surface near-tie. Only one choice reports both.
  • Winning everywhere is the wrong shape of claim. Choice C is true of the numbers and supports a general superiority, which is what the conclusion denies.
  • A true statement about the worst performer. Choice D is accurate and about the wrong coating.

Why A is wrong The zinc-rich plate went 7 to 8, which is barely a rise, so the generalization is technically true and hides the very difference the conclusion rests on.

Why B is right The conclusion is comparative in two directions at once. Choice B gives the edge contrast, 8% against 28 to 32, and the flat-surface cluster of 7 to 10 in which the primer's advantage nearly vanishes. That is exactly “chiefly at the plate edges rather than across flat surfaces.”

Why C is wrong True, and it argues for uniform superiority. The team's claim is that the advantage is concentrated at the edges, which this wording erases.

Why D is wrong The alkyd's performance is real and irrelevant. Nothing about the worst coating establishes where the best one gains its advantage.

stem_html:
Archaeologist Ines Vidal argues that the beads found at the Blombos Cave site were worn as ornaments rather than used as counters. She notes that the perforations show wear consistent with having been strung, and that the beads occur in clusters of similar size and color.

Which finding, if true, would most seriously weaken Vidal's argument?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Some Blombos beads show traces of ochre, a pigment used in the region for body decoration.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"Beads at a contemporaneous site 200 kilometers away show the same pattern of wear.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"C","content":"Counting devices from several later cultures consist of similarly sized beads strung on cord and sorted by color."},{"letter":"D","content":"The Blombos beads are made from a shell species that occurs naturally near the cave.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Weakening an argument means attacking the inference, not the facts. Vidal's facts — stringing wear, sorted clusters — are not in dispute. What can be attacked is whether those facts point only to ornament.
  • The choice that supports her is the easiest to misread as an attack. Ochre is decoration, so choice A strengthens the ornament reading; a student answering fast sees “traces” and treats any new complication as a weakness.
  • More of the same evidence is not counter-evidence. Choice B repeats her observation at another site.

Why A is wrong Ochre is used for body decoration, so this makes ornament more likely, not less. It is the choice most often taken by students who read for “new information” rather than for direction.

Why B is wrong It extends her observation geographically. If anything it supports the pattern she describes, and it certainly does not tell against her interpretation of it.

Why C is right Her inference runs from stringing wear and from the fact that the beads occur in clusters of similar size and color to the conclusion that they were ornaments. Choice C shows that known counting devices have exactly those two properties, so her evidence is equally consistent with the use she rejects, and the inference loses its force.

Why D is wrong Where the raw material came from bears on trade and procurement, not on what the finished beads were for.

stem_html:
In Aracelis Moreno's novel The Ledger, the narrator inherits her uncle's failing bakery and keeps its books meticulously. A critic claims that the narrator uses accounting as a way of avoiding her uncle's memory rather than honoring it.

Which quotation from The Ledger most effectively illustrates the critic's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"“He had kept the books in pencil, and I could not bring myself to erase a single figure.”","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"“The ovens were older than I was, and the left one ran hot in a way only he had known how to correct.”","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"C","content":"“Accounting, I told my sister, is the only kind of grief that adds up.”","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"D","content":"“I balanced the day's takings twice, and when they came out even the second time I started on the month, and then the year, until the room was dark and I had not once thought of him.”"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The quotation that names the theme is not the one that shows it. Choice C says grief and accounting in one breath, which is why it is chosen; naming the connection is not avoidance.
  • Preserving his handwriting is honoring, not avoiding. Choice A is the critic's claim in reverse.
  • Setting with feeling attached is still setting. Choice B remembers the uncle, which is the opposite of not thinking of him.

Why A is wrong Refusing to erase his pencil figures is an act of preservation. That illustrates honoring his memory, which is the reading the critic rejects.

Why B is wrong A description of the ovens that recalls his skill. Nothing here concerns the books or the avoidance the critic describes.

Why C is wrong It is an aphorism about grief and it connects the ledger to mourning directly, so it presents accounting as a form of grieving rather than an escape from it.

Why D is right The work expands to fill the day — takings, then the month, then the year — and the sentence ends on the point of it: the room was dark and she had not once thought of him. That is accounting used for avoiding her uncle's memory rather than honoring it, which is the critic's claim exactly.

stem_html:
The technique that Fanny Mendelssohn used in her Das Jahr—writing each movement on paper of a different color and pairing it with a line of poetry______ has no obvious precedent in the piano cycles of the period.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "—"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ",", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": ";", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": ":", "trap": "distant-antecedent"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Match the mark that opened. A dash opened the interruption twenty words earlier, so a dash has to close it. Every other choice leaves the pair unmatched.
  • The verb is a long way off. By the blank the reader has lost the subject “The technique,” and the sentence sounds as though a new clause is starting.
  • A semicolon needs a full clause after it. “has no obvious precedent” has no subject of its own, which is easy to miss because the interruption ends on a noun.

Why A is right It closes the dash pair, so the interruption is fenced off on both sides and the subject “The technique” joins its verb “has.”

Why B is wrong A comma cannot close what a dash opened. Mixing the two marks is the error this sentence is built to invite.

Why C is wrong A semicolon requires an independent clause on each side, and what follows is only a predicate.

Why D is wrong A colon would present what follows as an explanation or a list. What follows is the sentence's main verb, which cannot be introduced that way.

Between 1943 and 1946 the mathematician Grace Hopper worked on the Mark I at Harvard______ the machine's habit of failing overnight taught her more about programming than any lecture had.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":" where","trap":"distant-antecedent"},{"letter":"B","content":", where"},{"letter":"C","content":"and","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"D","content":"; and","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A restrictive “where” on a proper noun. Dropping the comma turns the clause into one that picks out which Harvard is meant, and there is only one.
  • “; and” looks extra careful. A semicolon with a conjunction is used for clauses that already contain commas; here it is heavier than the sentence can carry.
  • The unpunctuated relative reads smoothly. Choice A omits the comma before a nonrestrictive “where,” which the ear does not catch.

Why A is wrong Without the comma the “where” clause restricts “Harvard,” implying there is more than one Harvard and this is the relevant one.

Why B is right A comma before a nonrestrictive “where” attaches the second clause to Harvard, which is what the sentence means: the lesson came from working on that machine in that place.

Why C is wrong “And” can join two independent clauses, but a coordinating conjunction that joins them takes a comma in front of it, and none is offered here.

Why D is wrong A semicolon plus a conjunction is reserved for joining clauses that are themselves comma-heavy. Neither clause here is.

The question is no longer whether the rings of Saturn are young______ the icy particles are too bright to be four billion years old—but whether anything about their age can be measured without a spacecraft in orbit.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":";","trap":"comma-splice-plausible"},{"letter":"B","content":":","trap":"modifier-attachment"},{"letter":"C","content":"—"},{"letter":"D","content":",","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The closing mark is visible before the blank is filled. A dash appears later in the sentence, and it can only be the second half of a pair.
  • “Whether X but whether Y” is one structure. The interruption sits inside it, so the marks around it must be identical and must be a kind that can enclose.
  • The interrupting clause is independent. That makes a semicolon or colon feel possible, and neither can be closed by the dash that follows.

Why A is wrong A semicolon does not enclose; it separates. Opening with one and closing with a dash produces a sentence whose parenthesis has two different fences.

Why B is wrong A colon introduces and does not enclose, so the reader is given an explanation with no way back into the “but whether” that follows.

Why C is right It opens the pair the later dash closes, enclosing the parenthetical explanation and leaving “no longer whether … but whether” intact around it.

Why D is wrong A comma cannot pair with a dash, and it would leave an independent clause dangling inside a correlative structure.

  • The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in 2008 inside a mountain on a Norwegian island.
  • It stores duplicate samples of seeds held in other seed banks.
  • In 2015 researchers withdrew samples for the first time, to replace a collection lost in Aleppo.
  • The withdrawn samples were regrown and redeposited by 2020.
  • The vault holds no seeds that exist nowhere else.

The student wants to explain the vault's function to an audience unfamiliar with it. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"The Svalbard Global Seed Vault opened in 2008 inside a mountain on a Norwegian island, and it holds no seeds that exist nowhere else.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"In 2015 researchers withdrew samples from the Svalbard Global Seed Vault for the first time, and the withdrawn samples were regrown and redeposited by 2020.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"C","content":"Because the Svalbard Global Seed Vault stores duplicate samples, the seeds it holds also exist in other seed banks around the world.","trap":"true-but-irrelevant"},{"letter":"D","content":"The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, opened in 2008 inside a Norwegian mountain, is a backup: it holds duplicates of seeds kept in other banks, as when it supplied replacements for a collection lost in Aleppo."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A definition needs the purpose, not only the property. Choice C restates what duplication means and never says what the duplication is for.
  • The story is more memorable than the function. Choice B is the vault's one dramatic episode and explains nothing about what it is.
  • A negative fact is a poor introduction. Choice A tells a newcomer what the vault does not have.

Why A is wrong Location and a negative property. A reader who did not know what the vault was still would not.

Why B is wrong An episode without its purpose. Withdrawal and redeposit only make sense once the backup role has been stated.

Why C is wrong It says duplicates are duplicates. True, circular, and silent about why anyone would build a mountain vault for them.

Why D is right It gives the newcomer the category first — a backup — then the mechanism, duplicates of seeds kept in other banks, then the one case that shows the mechanism working. That is what explaining a function to an unfamiliar audience requires.

The student wants to emphasize the delay between Price's achievements and their recognition. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

Traps in this question

  • A delay needs two dates. Only one choice names both ends of the gap, and the others each fix on a single moment.
  • Neglect is not delay. Choice B describes rejection and rediscovery, which is a story about obstacles rather than about elapsed time.

Why A is right 1933 and 2018 are the two ends of the gap, and “sixty-five years after her death” states the delay outright. “Although” puts the achievement and the wait in the same sentence, which is what the goal asks for.

Why B is wrong Rejection and rediscovery are both real, and together they describe neglect rather than a measurable interval between achievement and recognition.

Why C is wrong A single fact about the 2009 find, with no achievement dated against it.

Why D is wrong It supplies the rediscovery and the concertos but no earlier point to measure from, so nothing is shown to have been delayed.

Traps in this question

The gesture is often read as a step toward returning contested items. ______ publication and restitution are separate decisions: a museum can document an object's route out of its country of origin in complete detail and still decline every request to send it back.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Therefore,","trap":"transition-reversal"},{"letter":"B","content":"Meanwhile,","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"In fact,"},{"letter":"D","content":"Likewise,","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The sentence corrects a common reading. It does not merely contrast; it says what is actually the case against what the gesture is taken to mean, which is what “in fact” marks.
  • A causal transition would endorse the misreading. “Therefore” makes separateness follow from the hopeful reading, which is the reverse of the argument.
  • “Meanwhile” sounds neutral and says nothing. It marks simultaneity, and no two things here happen at the same time.

Why A is wrong Causal and reversed. Nothing about the gesture being read as a step toward return implies that the two decisions are separate.

Why B is wrong Temporal. There is no second timeline running alongside the first for it to mark.

Why C is right The blank sits between a widespread interpretation and its correction. The last sentence asserts what is really so, that publication and restitution are separate decisions, and a corrective transition is the one that fits.

Why D is wrong Additive. It would make the correction another example of the hopeful reading rather than a challenge to it.

stem_html:
A drug that reduces a symptom is not always a drug that treats a disease. Statins lower cholesterol and also lower heart attacks, so the symptom and the outcome move together. ______ torcetrapib raised the so-called good cholesterol substantially in trials and increased deaths, which is why regulators now ask for outcome data rather than marker data.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"Consequently,","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"Similarly,","trap":"transition-reversal"},{"letter":"C","content":"Granted,","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"D","content":"By contrast,"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two examples, opposite lessons. Statins are the case where marker and outcome agree; torcetrapib is the case where they part. Any transition that links them as alike fails.
  • “Similarly” is the trap of surface form. Both sentences describe a drug and a cholesterol measure, so they look parallel until you read what happened.
  • The closing clause invites a causal reading. “which is why regulators now ask” supplies the consequence inside the sentence, so the transition does not need to.

Why A is wrong Causal. The torcetrapib result does not follow from the statin result, and the sentence already carries its own consequence in the final clause.

Why B is wrong It asserts that the two cases teach the same lesson, which is exactly what the paragraph is written to deny.

Why C is wrong Concessive. It would frame torcetrapib as a point conceded to an opponent, and no opposing position has been introduced.

Why D is right The torcetrapib case is the counterexample to the statin case: the marker improved and the outcome got worse. A contrastive transition is the only kind that marks a reversal between two examples.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2020 essay on translation.

A translator's first duty is often described as fidelity, and the word is doing more work than it can carry. Fidelity to what: the author's sentences, the author's effect on a first reader, or the effect those sentences would have had if the author had written in the second language? These are three different books. The choice among them is not a failure of nerve to be avoided but the act of translating itself.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It breaks a single term into incompatible senses, preparing the essay's claim that choosing among them is what translation is."},{"letter":"B","content":"It concedes that translators frequently fail to achieve fidelity of any kind.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"C","content":"It offers three examples of successful translation for the reader to compare.","trap":"wrong-part-of-passage"},{"letter":"D","content":"It poses a question the essay will answer by choosing one kind of fidelity over the others.","trap":"half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A question in the text is not always a question the text answers. The essay's closing sentence refuses to rank the three, so a choice promising an answer describes a different essay.
  • The function of a sentence is fixed by what follows it. “These are three different books” and the sentence after it are what the underlined question exists to set up.
  • Failure is mentioned and denied. The last sentence calls the choice not a failure of nerve, which rules out the concession reading.

Why A is right The sentence splits “fidelity” into three senses that cannot all be honored at once, which is what licenses the next sentence, “These are three different books,” and the claim that the choice is translation itself.

Why B is wrong No claim about how often translators fail appears anywhere in the text.

Why C is wrong The three items are senses of a word, not translations, and none is offered as successful or otherwise.

Why D is wrong The essay declines to choose. Its conclusion is that the choice among them is the act of translating, not that one kind of fidelity wins.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2017 article on animal cognition.

Reports that an octopus recognizes individual keepers are usually met with a demand for controls, and rightly so. But the demand is applied unevenly. No one asks for a controlled trial before accepting that a dog knows its owner, and the reason is not that the dog evidence is stronger. It is that the claim about the dog costs us nothing to believe.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"It surveys the evidence for octopus recognition and finds it insufficient.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"B","content":"It endorses a standard of evidence, then argues that the standard is applied selectively for reasons unrelated to evidence."},{"letter":"C","content":"It rejects a standard of evidence as too demanding for research on invertebrates.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"It compares two species and concludes that one is more cognitively capable than the other.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Rightly so” is the load-bearing phrase. The writer accepts the demand for controls, so any choice that has the standard rejected contradicts the second clause of the first sentence.
  • The passage is about us, not about octopuses. Its conclusion concerns what we find cheap to believe, and two choices treat it as a claim about animals.

Why A is wrong The evidence for octopus recognition is never weighed. The subject is our differing standards for weighing it.

Why B is right The first sentence grants the standard, and the rest shows it is not applied to dogs, ending on the reason: the claim about the dog costs us nothing to believe. Endorsement followed by a charge of selective application.

Why C is wrong The text says the demand for controls is right. Its complaint is unevenness, not severity.

Why D is wrong No comparison of cognitive capacity is made. The dog appears only as a case we accept without controls.

stem_html:
To test whether a bird's song is learned, researchers raise nestlings without hearing adults of their species. Zebra finches raised this way produce abnormal songs, and when such isolates are housed together for several generations, each generation's song moves closer to the wild form, arriving at it by about the fourth. This result indicates that the wild song is shaped ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"by the first isolate generation's abnormal song, which later generations copy faithfully.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"B","content":"entirely by a genetic program that does not require hearing other birds.","trap":"too-extreme"},{"letter":"C","content":"by biases in learning and production that steer song toward a particular form across generations even when no model is available at the start."},{"letter":"D","content":"by the acoustics of the enclosures in which the isolates were housed.","trap":"out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The first result and the second point different ways. Isolation produces abnormal song, which argues for learning; the drift back to the wild form argues for something innate. The answer must hold both.
  • The absolute is refuted by the first sentence. If the song were entirely genetic, the isolates' first-generation song would already be normal.
  • Faithful copying cannot explain change. Choice A describes a process that would freeze the abnormal song, and the passage reports it moving.

Why A is wrong Faithful copying of the first abnormal song predicts that the abnormality persists. The passage reports the opposite: each generation moves closer to the wild form.

Why B is wrong Contradicted by the finding that zebra finches raised without adults produce abnormal songs. A purely genetic program would not need a model at all.

Why C is right It accounts for both halves. Learning is needed, since the first isolates sing abnormally, and the target is not arbitrary, since successive generations converge on the wild form without ever hearing it. Biases in learning and production are what carry the song there.

Why D is wrong Enclosure acoustics are never mentioned, and they would not explain why the drift ends at the wild form specifically.

stem_html:
An economist examined tipping in two American cities where a law raised the minimum wage for restaurant servers to match that of other workers. In both cities, average tips as a percentage of the bill fell after the change, but total server earnings rose. The economist concluded that diners' tipping responds to ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"the size of the bill, which rose in both cities after the law took effect.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"the quality of service, which declined once servers were paid more.","trap":"half-right"},{"letter":"C","content":"changes in the law that they are unlikely to have been aware of.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"their beliefs about how much servers are already paid, rather than to service quality alone."}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A percentage falling while a total rises. Both facts are given, and a choice that explains only one of them will feel complete.
  • The insulting explanation is available. Choice B blames servers, and nothing in the passage measures service at all.
  • Awareness is the hinge. Choice C says diners did not know about the law, which would leave the change in tipping unexplained.

Why A is wrong The passage never reports bill sizes rising, and a larger bill with an unchanged percentage would leave the percentage unchanged, which is not what happened.

Why B is wrong Service quality is not measured anywhere in the study. Asserting a decline imports an explanation the evidence does not contain.

Why C is wrong If diners were unaware of the law, their tipping could not respond to it, and the observed change would need some other cause.

Why D is right Average tips as a percentage of the bill fell when server pay changed and nothing else in the passage did, so the percentage is responding to something other than the meal itself. Beliefs about how much servers are already paid is the only offered factor that the law would alter.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2018 article about urban rivers.

When a buried river is daylighted — dug up and returned to the surface — the result is usually described as restoration. The word flatters the work. What returns is a channel of the right shape carrying water of the right chemistry, and that is a real achievement; what does not return is the floodplain, which the city has been built across and cannot give back. Cities that understand this build for a river that will have nowhere to go in a flood. Cities that believe the word build parks.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Daylighting recovers a river's channel and water quality but not its floodplain, and cities that recognize the difference plan differently."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Daylighting is a form of restoration that has been undervalued by city planners.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Cities that daylight rivers should stop building parks along them.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The chemistry of a daylighted river's water usually matches that of the original.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The passage praises and withholds in the same breath. It calls the channel and chemistry a real achievement, which makes a wholly positive reading available to a fast reader.
  • The last two sentences are the argument. The contrast between cities that understand this and cities that believe the word is where the main idea lives.
  • A supporting clause offered as the point. Water chemistry is one item in a list, not the claim.

Why A is right The text grants what daylighting recovers, names what it cannot — the floodplain the city has been built across — and closes on the planning consequence of taking that seriously.

Why B is wrong The passage argues that the word restoration flatters the work, which is the opposite of saying daylighting is undervalued.

Why C is wrong Parks appear in one clause as a symptom of the mistaken view. The text issues no recommendation about building them.

Why D is wrong A detail from the middle of the passage, offered as evidence for the achievement, not as the idea the text is organized around.

stem_html:
Text 1

The replication crisis is often told as a story about statistics, and the fixes proposed are statistical: larger samples, preregistration, stricter thresholds. But a study can be preregistered, powered and still measure the wrong thing. The deeper problem is that many constructs in psychology are defined by the instruments used to measure them, so a failed replication cannot tell you whether the effect is absent or the instrument has drifted.

Text 2

Critics who say the crisis is about measurement rather than statistics are describing a problem that statistical reform reveals rather than hides. Before preregistration, an instrument that measured the wrong construct produced publishable results indefinitely; now it produces a conspicuous string of failures. The reforms did not solve the measurement problem, but they are how we came to see it.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1 about statistical fixes?
choices_json: [{"letter":"A","content":"By claiming that the replication crisis has been exaggerated by critics of psychology.","trap":"out-of-scope"},{"letter":"B","content":"By agreeing that measurement is the deeper problem while arguing that the statistical reforms are what made it visible."},{"letter":"C","content":"By arguing that preregistration and larger samples do in fact resolve the ambiguity of a failed replication.","trap":"reversed-relationship"},{"letter":"D","content":"By conceding that psychological constructs cannot be measured and that reform is therefore pointless.","trap":"too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Agreement and disagreement in one response. Text 2 accepts Text 1's diagnosis and rejects its implied verdict on the reforms, and choices that pick only one half of that are the traps.
  • The sentence that looks like a concession is the argument. “The reforms did not solve the measurement problem” agrees with Text 1; the clause after it is where Text 2 makes its case.
  • Overshooting into nihilism. Text 1 never says constructs cannot be measured, and Text 2 never says reform is pointless.

Why A is wrong Text 2 treats the crisis as real; its disagreement with Text 1 is about what the statistical reforms accomplished.

Why B is right Text 2 grants that the reforms did not solve the measurement problem, which is Text 1's point, and then claims they are how we came to see it, which is a defense of the fixes Text 1 treats as beside the point.

Why C is wrong Text 2 says the opposite in its final sentence. It does not claim the reforms resolve the ambiguity, only that they expose it.

Why D is wrong Neither text says measurement is impossible, and Text 2's whole purpose is to defend the value of reform.
